# Build a lifecycle flow

## Purpose
One procedure runs every flow build. The flow type picks the sub-skill; the shape of the
job (confirm trigger, set filters, map steps, draft copy, check discount, assemble brief)
never changes.

## Steps
1. Read the idea or trigger and name the flow type (welcome, browse-cart-abandon,
   post-purchase, win-back, sunset, back-in-stock, replenishment, loyalty-vip).
2. Load the matching sub-skill for that type; it owns the timing and content logic.
3. Confirm the trigger event actually fires in this store's data before building around it.
4. Set entry, exit and re-entry filters against every other live flow.
5. Map delay, channel and purpose per step using the sub-skill's rule.
6. Draft copy per step and channel via life/message; claim-check every step.
7. Set discount eligibility, if any, via life/discount-policy-check.
8. Assemble the flow brief and run the LIFE self-QA checklist.

## Checks
Trigger confirmed. No stage overlap with another flow. Every claim checked. Output
matches the flow-brief shape exactly.

## Output
A flow brief ready for the founder gate, plus the registry stub for the read point.

## Example
Idea: "Win-back flow underperforms; rebuild timing off purchase cadence." Output: a
3-email, 2-SMS win-back brief entering at 1.5x the customer's own average order gap,
exiting on purchase, no discount until email 3, read point 45 days post-launch.

# Email message drafting

## Purpose
Writes the email-specific fields a flow or campaign step needs: subject line,
preview text, body and CTA, none of which SMS or WhatsApp carry, and flags any
spam-trigger language before the draft reaches life/deliverability-audit. Email
is still the channel that carries the most product detail and dynamic content, so
this skill also marks where a dynamic block (cart contents, recommended products)
belongs for the build step that follows.

## Steps
1. Write the subject line and the preview text as two separate, complementary
   lines; the preview should add information, not repeat the subject.
2. Write the body at a skimmable length with exactly one clear call to action,
   never two competing links fighting for the same click.
3. Mark where a dynamic product block or personalised image belongs, so the
   email-build step can wire it correctly.
4. Screen the subject line for spam-trigger words, ALL-CAPS and excess
   punctuation before handing the draft on.

## Checks
Subject and preview are both written, never left blank. Exactly one CTA per
email. No unscreened spam-trigger language reaches the build step.

## Output
{subject, preview, body, cta, dynamic_block_ref}

## Example
Subject: "Your Aria necklace is still here." Preview: "Free shipping ends
tonight." Body: three short lines, one button reading "Finish my order," with a
dynamic_block_ref pointing at the customer's actual saved cart.

# SMS message drafting

## Purpose
Writes short, compliant SMS copy for a flow or campaign step: brand name up
front, a single link, and the opt-out instruction consent-governance requires,
all inside the quiet-hours window and cadence cap life/channel-policy has
already set for this brand and market. SMS earns its place through urgency and
brevity, not through carrying the same content an email already sent.

## Steps
1. Draft the message inside a carrier-friendly character length, with one link
   at most; a second link splits attention and often breaks link shortening.
2. Put the brand name at the very start of the message and add the opt-out
   instruction at the end, per the consent-governance rule for this market.
3. Check the scheduled send time against the quiet-hours window and the
   per-customer weekly cadence cap before it is queued.
4. Cut any factual claim that cannot be stated accurately inside the space
   available, rather than compressing it into something misleading.

## Checks
Opt-out instruction is present on every send. Quiet hours are respected for the
recipient's own market. Exactly one link appears in the message.

## Output
{body, link, opt_out_line}

## Example
"[Brand] Still want the Aria necklace? Your cart's saved: [link]. Reply STOP to
opt out." - one link, brand-first, opt-out included, sent inside quiet hours.

# Subscription offer and cancel-flow design

## Purpose
Makes the reason to subscribe stronger than a flat discount, and designs a cancel
flow that is as easy to complete as sign-up but tries a reason-matched
alternative and a costed save offer before the subscriber leaves.

1. Compare the subscription's total value (price, perks, flexibility) against the
   plain discount it replaces, in real numbers.

   spend line.
3. Build the cancel flow as four stages: benefit reminder, exit-reason survey, a
   reason-matched alternative (pause, swap, frequency change), then a conditional,
   costed save offer only if earlier stages fail.
4. Cost the save offer against the subscriber's own order count and value.
5. Cap pause/skip/delay abuse without breaking a genuine flexibility need.
6. Add non-monetary mechanics (streaks, milestone gifts) as an addition, tested
   against a discount-only save, not assumed superior.
7. Set per-stage save-rate tracking so a weak stage can be rewritten specifically.

## Checks
Cancel is as easy to complete as sign-up. Save offer sized in code to the
subscriber's own value. Non-monetary mechanic tested, not assumed.

## Output
A subscription offer spec and a four-stage cancel-flow design with per-stage
save-rate targets.

"Stage 3 (reason: 'too much product') offers a frequency change to every 8 weeks,
not a discount; only subscribers who still exit reach stage 4's 15% save offer."

# Branded customer community design

## Purpose
Checks whether a peer-to-peer, always-on community actually fits the brand's
repeat-buyer base before building one, then designs the structure, moderation and
a light engagement calendar distinct from the campaign calendar and the support
inbox.

## Steps
1. Check the brand's repeat, high-engagement buyer count and engagement level
   against what sustains a community; recommend go or no-go with the evidence.
2. Choose the platform (Slack, Discord, Circle) and design the channel structure
   around named use cases (product help, early access, feedback).
3. Write the moderation policy, especially how a public complaint routes to the
   real support queue instead of being handled in public.
4. Build a light, sustainable engagement calendar (prompts, early-access drops,
   AMAs), distinct from the weekly campaign calendar.
5. Set when a founder or team member should show up in person versus stay quiet.
6. Set the path for a recurring community theme to reach the VoC record.
7. Track membership, active-member share, and the repeat-purchase rate of
   members versus non-members, in code.

## Checks
Go/no-go is grounded in real evidence, not enthusiasm. Complaints always route to
support. Member-vs-non-member comparison computed in code.

## Output
A community structure and moderation policy, an engagement calendar, and a
recurring health note.

## Example
"1,400 repeat buyers, 30% opened last 3 emails - enough base to test. Discord,
3 channels (help, early-access, feedback). Members' repeat-purchase rate tracked
against a matched non-member cohort from launch."
